guide.description: awk splits each input line into whitespace-separated fields and lets you print any of them by number: $1 is the first field, $2 the second, and so on ($0 means the whole line). It's the tool for pulling one column out of column-shaped text without reaching for a full parser.

flags.desc: use <sep> as the field separator instead of whitespace

exercises.title: Pull a field with awk
exercises.task: access.log's lines look like '200 GET /home' — $1 is the status code. Print just the status code from every line.

access.log.content:
200 GET /home
404 GET /missing
200 GET /about
500 GET /api/users
200 GET /home
404 GET /old-page

hints: awk '{print $N}' <file> prints field N of every line
The status code is the first field, so N is 1

exercises.title: Pull a different field
exercises.task: $N works for any field, not just $1 — print the third field ($3), the URL path, from every line.

access.log.content:
200 GET /home
404 GET /missing
200 GET /about
500 GET /api/users
200 GET /home
404 GET /old-page

hints: Same command shape, just change which field number you print
The path is the third whitespace-separated field

exercises.title: Print multiple fields
exercises.task: List multiple field numbers separated by a comma to print more than one column. Print the status code and the path together ($1 then $3) from every line.

access.log.content:
200 GET /home
404 GET /missing
200 GET /about
500 GET /api/users
200 GET /home
404 GET /old-page

hints: List field numbers separated by a comma to print more than one
Status code first, then path — in that order
